help.title: Dendrogram
help.body:
What is a dendrogram?
A dendrogram is a tree diagram that shows how individual observations (rows) get grouped together based on how similar they are. The chart is built by an algorithm that repeatedly asks "of everything left, which two things are most alike right now?" and merges them - then repeats, until everything has merged into one group.

Each vertical line joining upward is a merge point. The height at which two branches join tells you how different they were when they merged: a low merge means the two items are nearly identical; a high merge means they were only combined because, eventually, everything has to join up. Cutting the tree at a chosen height (or a chosen number of clusters, "k") splits it into distinct groups.

Purpose
Unlike a test such as ANOVA, a dendrogram does not require you to already know the groups in your data. It is exploratory: it looks across every selected variable at once and lets a grouping structure emerge on its own, which you can then investigate, validate against known labels, or use to decide how many groups actually exist.

Manufacturing example
Cluster machines or production batches using sensor readings (temperature, vibration, spindle speed, cycle time, defect rate, etc.). Batches or machines that behave similarly will merge at low heights. If two machines that are supposed to run an identical process end up in very different branches, that can flag a miscalibration or a wear issue worth investigating. Clustering incoming material batches by composition or strength can similarly flag an unusual batch worth inspecting before it reaches the line.

Non-manufacturing example
Cluster customers using purchase behavior (spend, frequency, categories purchased) to find natural customer segments without deciding the segments in advance; or cluster survey respondents by their answers to find groups of people who respond similarly, before doing any further demographic analysis.

Dialog inputs

Variable(s) to cluster (numeric)
The numeric variables used to measure how similar/different each row is. These drive the entire tree shape. Include variables that are actually relevant to the grouping you're investigating - unrelated variables can dilute or distort the result.

Label variable (optional - e.g. Batch ID)
An identifier column (e.g. a Batch ID, Machine ID, or name) used only to label the leaves on the chart and in the output tables. It is not used in the distance/cluster calculation. If left blank, leaves are labeled with their row number in the dataset.

Standardize variables before clustering (z-score)
When checked, every selected variable is rescaled to a common z-score scale (mean 0, standard deviation 1) before distances are calculated. This is recommended whenever your variables are on different units or scales (e.g. RPM in the thousands next to a temperature in tens of degrees) - otherwise the variable with the largest raw numbers will dominate the clustering regardless of how meaningful it actually is.

Distance measure
How "different" two rows are calculated from their variable values. Options:
  • euclidean - straight-line distance; the most common default choice.
  • manhattan - sum of absolute differences across variables; less sensitive to large outliers than euclidean.
  • maximum - the single largest difference across all variables.
  • canberra - a weighted version of manhattan distance that is more sensitive to differences near zero; useful when variables include small counts or rates.
  • minkowski - a generalized distance that includes euclidean and manhattan as special cases.
Linkage method
How the distance between two groups (not just two individual rows) is calculated as the tree is built. Options:
  • ward.D2 - merges groups to minimize the increase in total within-group variance; tends to produce compact, evenly-sized clusters. A common default.
  • complete - distance between groups is the distance between their two most different members; tends to produce compact clusters with clear separation.
  • average - distance between groups is the average distance across all pairs of members; a middle ground between complete and single linkage.
  • single - distance between groups is the distance between their two closest members; can produce long, "chained" clusters.
  • centroid - distance between groups is the distance between their average (centroid) points.
  • median - similar to centroid, using a different update rule for merged groups.
  • mcquitty - a weighted average distance between groups.
Color/box branches by cluster
When checked, the tree is cut into the number of clusters specified below and each resulting branch and its leaf labels are colored accordingly, making the groups visually easy to distinguish. When unchecked, the whole tree is drawn in a single color.

Number of clusters to highlight (k)
How many groups to cut the tree into. This value is used both for coloring the plot (if enabled above) and for assigning the cluster membership tables further below - so the picture and the tables always agree with each other.

Draw dendrogram horizontally
When checked, the tree is drawn sideways (leaves along the left, root on the right) instead of the default top-down orientation. This can help readability when there are many leaves, since labels then run down the side rather than needing to be rotated.

Show leaf labels
Toggles whether individual leaf labels are drawn at all. For very large trees (many dozens of rows), even a small font can become unreadable in a fixed-width chart; unchecking this keeps the branch/cluster structure and colors visible without the clutter of illegible text.

Leaf label font size (leave blank for automatic sizing)
Font size for leaf labels. Left blank, the size is calculated automatically based on how many leaves are in the tree, so larger trees automatically get smaller labels. Enter a number to override this and use a fixed size instead.

Leaf label angle (degrees)
Rotation angle for leaf labels, from 0 (horizontal) to 90 (vertical). Higher angles fit more labels into the same width; 45 degrees is often a good compromise between fitting many labels and keeping them easy to read.

Cluster membership tables to display
Adds data table(s) below the chart showing which rows fall into which cluster, including every original column in your dataset (not just the ones used for clustering). Rows are ordered to match the chart's left-to-right leaf order, and cluster numbers are renumbered so cluster 1 is whichever group appears first (leftmost) in the chart. Options:
  • None - no table is produced.
  • Combined - a single table of all clustered rows with a "DendroCluster" column added.
  • PerCluster - a separate table for each cluster, each showing only the rows belonging to that group.
Show summary statistics per cluster
When checked, produces one table per clustering variable showing, for each cluster: n (cluster size), mean, standard deviation, median, minimum, and maximum. Values are reported on the original (unstandardized) scale so they are in real units, even when standardization is enabled for the clustering itself. This is the quickest way to understand why the clusters differ - e.g. which variable separates cluster 1 from cluster 2, and by how much.

Enter a chart title
Optional custom title displayed above the chart. If left blank, the chart is titled "Dendrogram".

Requires the dendextend package. For detailed help use R help(hclust, package = 'stats'), help(dist, package = 'stats'), or help(as.ggdend, package = 'dendextend').
